GitHub Issue:
Post Date: 2017-01-10T05:24:30Z
Current Date: April 4 2025
Title: Single file @Table definition order is important
Description: It is worth nothing, that if you define all of your Entities (i.e. @Table classes) in a single file, that the order is important. If you reference a Entity as part of a relation (i.e. @OneToOne) before that referenced Entity is defined, you'll receive an error like below:

```
/Users/Danijel/projects/am/am-api/lib/model/model.js:175
[1]     __metadata("design:type", StoreBillingPlan)
[1]                               ^
[1]
[1] ReferenceError: StoreBillingPlan is not defined
[1]     at Object.<anonymous> (/Users/x/projects/am/am-api/lib/model/model.js:175:31)
[1]     at Module._compile (module.js:571:32)
[1]     at Object.Module._extensions..js (module.js:580:10)
[1]     at Module.load (module.js:488:32)
[1]     at tryModuleLoad (module.js:447:12)
[1]     at Function.Module._load (module.js:439:3)
[1]     at Module.require (module.js:498:17)
[1]     at require (internal/module.js:20:19)
[1]     at Object.<anonymous> (/Users/x/projects/am/am-api/lib/services/auth.js:10:17)
[1]     at Module._compile (module.js:571:32)
```

In my case, defining StoreBillingPlan before the above code was run solved my issue.  Is it possible to make order not important? 

Note: For those splitting Entities across files this shouldn't be an issue. 

You must provide a category number (1-3). Your response must follow this format exactly:

CATEGORY: [category number]
REASONING: [your reasoning here, including specific reasons why an issue would be hard to dockerize if choosing category 3]
llm_response:
I'll analyze this GitHub issue to determine if a build environment is needed to verify the solution.

CATEGORY: 1
REASONING: This issue is about a reference error that occurs when TypeScript entity classes with decorators like @Table and @OneToOne are defined in a specific order within a single file. The problem and solution are clearly described: when referencing an entity class before it's defined, a ReferenceError occurs, and the solution is to reorder the class definitions. This is a conceptual issue related to how JavaScript/TypeScript handles class references and how the TypeORM (or similar ORM) decorators work. The solution can be verified through code analysis without needing to build or run the code. An LLM can understand that this is a standard behavior in JavaScript where variables/classes must be defined before they're used. No build environment is necessary to verify that reordering class definitions would solve the reference error, as this is a fundamental language behavior that can be analyzed statically.
